Before you conclude, ensure that we run the experience improvement through a Steve Jobs pass (he needs to approve, so iterate until he would).

<skill_content name="brainstorming">
# Skill: brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

1: /**
2:  * Feature flags for the studio client.
3:  *
4:  * A flag is resolved once per read, highest precedence first:
5:  *
6:  *   1. `?flags=<name>:<value>`      — QA and demos without a rebuild
7:  *   2. `localStorage["studio.flags.<name>"]`
8:  *   3. `VITE_STUDIO_<NAME>` env variable
9:  *   4. the flag's declared default
10:  *
11:  * Unknown values fall through to the next source, so a typo in a query string
12:  * can never silently change behaviour.
13:  */
14: 
15: export type FeatureFlagName = "firstRunWizard";
16: 
17: export interface FeatureFlagDefinition {
18:   name: FeatureFlagName;
19:   description: string;
20:   envVar: string;
21:   defaultEnabled: boolean;
22: }
23: 
24: export const FEATURE_FLAGS: Record<FeatureFlagName, FeatureFlagDefinition> = {
25:   firstRunWizard: {
26:     name: "firstRunWizard",
27:     description: "Guided first-run tour for new Living Studio users.",
28:     envVar: "VITE_STUDIO_FIRST_RUN_WIZARD",
29:     defaultEnabled: true,
30:   },
31: };
32: 
33: export const FLAG_STORAGE_PREFIX = "studio.flags.";
34: export const FLAG_QUERY_PARAM = "flags";
35: 
36: export type FlagSource = "query" | "storage" | "env" | "default";
37: 
38: export interface ResolvedFlag {
39:   enabled: boolean;
40:   source: FlagSource;
41:   raw: string | null;
42: }
43: 
44: /** Values a human might reasonably type. Everything else is "not set". */
45: export interface FlagSources {
46:   env?: string | null;
47:   stored?: string | null;
48:   query?: string | null;
49: }
50: 
51: const TRUTHY = new Set(["1", "true", "on", "yes", "enabled"]);
52: const FALSY = new Set(["0", "false", "off", "no", "disabled"]);
53: 
54: export function parseFlagValue(raw: string | null | undefined): boolean | null {
55:   if (raw === null || raw === undefined) {
56:     return null;
57:   }
58:   const normalized = raw.trim().toLowerCase();
59:   if (TRUTHY.has(normalized)) {
60:     return true;
61:   }
62:   if (FALSY.has(normalized)) {
63:     return false;
64:   }
65:   return null;
66: }
67: 
68: function readEnvFlag(definition: FeatureFlagDefinition): string | null {
69:   const env = import.meta.env as Record<string, unknown>;
70:   const raw = env[definition.envVar];
71:   if (raw === undefined || raw === null) {
72:     return null;
73:   }
74:   return String(raw);
75: }
76: 
77: function readStoredFlag(definition: FeatureFlagDefinition): string | null {
78:   if (typeof window === "undefined") {
79:     return null;
80:   }
81:   try {
82:     return window.localStorage.getItem(`${FLAG_STORAGE_PREFIX}${definition.name}`);
83:   } catch {
84:     // Private browsing modes can deny storage access.
85:     return null;
86:   }
87: }
88: 
89: /** `?flags=firstRunWizard:off,otherFlag:on` */
90: function readQueryFlag(definition: FeatureFlagDefinition): string | null {
91:   if (typeof window === "undefined") {
92:     return null;
93:   }
94:   const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search);
95:   for (const group of params.getAll(FLAG_QUERY_PARAM)) {
96:     for (const pair of group.split(",")) {
97:       const separator = pair.indexOf(":");
98:       if (separator === -1) {
99:         continue;
100:       }
101:       const name = pair.slice(0, separator).trim();
102:       if (name !== definition.name) {
103:         continue;
104:       }
105:       const value = pair.slice(separator + 1).trim();
106:       if (value) {
107:         return value;
108:       }
109:     }
110:   }
111:   return null;
112: }
113: 
114: function defaultSources(definition: FeatureFlagDefinition): Required<FlagSources> {
115:   return {
116:     query: readQueryFlag(definition),
117:     stored: readStoredFlag(definition),
118:     env: readEnvFlag(definition),
119:   };
120: }
121: 
122: export function resolveFlag(
123:   name: FeatureFlagName,
124:   sources?: FlagSources,
125: ): ResolvedFlag {
126:   const definition = FEATURE_FLAGS[name];
127:   const resolved = sources ?? defaultSources(definition);
128: 
129:   const candidates: { source: FlagSource; raw: string | null | undefined }[] = [
130:     { source: "query", raw: resolved.query },
131:     { source: "storage", raw: resolved.stored },
132:     { source: "env", raw: resolved.env },
133:   ];
134: 
135:   for (const candidate of candidates) {
136:     const parsed = parseFlagValue(candidate.raw);
137:     if (parsed !== null) {
138:       return { enabled: parsed, source: candidate.source, raw: candidate.raw ?? null };
139:     }
140:   }
141: 
142:   return { enabled: definition.defaultEnabled, source: "default", raw: null };
143: }
144: 
145: export function isFeatureEnabled(name: FeatureFlagName, sources?: FlagSources): boolean {
146:   return resolveFlag(name, sources).enabled;
147: }
148: 
149: /** Persist a local override. Pass `null` to fall back to env/default. */
150: export function setFeatureOverride(name: FeatureFlagName, enabled: boolean | null): void {
151:   if (typeof window === "undefined") {
152:     return;
153:   }
154:   const key = `${FLAG_STORAGE_PREFIX}${name}`;
155:   try {
156:     if (enabled === null) {
157:       window.localStorage.removeItem(key);
158:       return;
159:     }
160:     window.localStorage.setItem(key, enabled ? "on" : "off");
161:   } catch {
162:     // Storage is an optimisation here; the flag still resolves from env/default.
163:   }
164: }
165: 
166: export function clearFeatureOverride(name: FeatureFlagName): void {
167:   setFeatureOverride(name, null);
168: }

3: /**
4:  * Pure flow rules for the first-run tour. No React, no storage, no DOM — the
5:  * whole sequence can be reasoned about and tested as plain functions.
6:  */
7: 
8: export const ONBOARDING_VERSION = 1;
9: export const LAST_STEP_INDEX = STEPS.length - 1;
10: 
11: export type OnboardingStatus = "pending" | "active" | "done" | "skipped";
12: 
13: export interface OnboardingState {
14:   status: OnboardingStatus;
15:   step: number;
16:   goal: GoalId | null;
17:   version: number;
18: }
19: 
20: export function createOnboardingState(
21:   overrides: Partial<OnboardingState> = {},
22: ): OnboardingState {
23:   return {
24:     status: "pending",
25:     step: 0,
26:     goal: null,
27:     version: ONBOARDING_VERSION,
28:     ...overrides,
29:   };
30: }
31: 
32: export function clampStep(step: number): number {
33:   if (!Number.isFinite(step)) {
34:     return 0;
35:   }
36:   return Math.min(LAST_STEP_INDEX, Math.max(0, Math.trunc(step)));
37: }
38: 
39: export function stepAt(step: number): WizardStepId {
40:   return STEPS[clampStep(step)].id;
41: }
42: 
43: /** A tour the user has neither finished nor skipped should greet them. */
44: export function shouldAutoOpen(state: OnboardingState): boolean {
45:   return state.status === "pending" || state.status === "active";
46: }
47: 
48: export function isFinished(state: OnboardingState): boolean {
49:   return state.status === "done" || state.status === "skipped";
50: }
51: 
52: /** Replay: start from the top, forget the previous choice. */
53: export function startTour(state: OnboardingState): OnboardingState {
54:   return { ...state, status: "active", step: 0, goal: null };
55: }
56: 
57: export function advanceTour(state: OnboardingState): OnboardingState {
58:   if (isFinished(state)) {
59:     return state;
60:   }
61:   // The flow will not leave the starting-point step without a choice.
62:   if (state.step === GOAL_STEP_INDEX && state.goal === null) {
63:     return state;
64:   }
65:   return { ...state, status: "active", step: clampStep(state.step + 1) };
66: }
67: 
68: export function retreatTour(state: OnboardingState): OnboardingState {
69:   if (isFinished(state)) {
70:     return state;
71:   }
72:   return { ...state, status: "active", step: clampStep(state.step - 1) };
73: }

76:   return { ...state, goal };

80:   return { ...state, status: "done", step: LAST_STEP_INDEX };
81: }

19: export const UiActionContext = createContext<UiActionDispatcher | null>(null);
20: 
21: export function useUiActions(): UiActionDispatcher | null {

23: }

26:  * Props arrive already validated, but this stays defensive: a malformed action
27:  * is dropped rather than allowed to break the card that holds it.
28:  */
29: export function readActions(props: Record<string, unknown>): UiAction[] {
30:   const raw = props.actions;
31:   if (!Array.isArray(raw)) {
32:     return [];
33:   }
34: 
35:   const actions: UiAction[] = [];
36:   for (const entry of raw) {
37:     if (typeof entry !== "object" || entry === null) {
38:       continue;

45:       label: candidate.label,

48:     });
49:   }
50:   return actions;

1: # Agentic ODI - AI Developer Guardrails
2: 
3: This file provides system instructions and guardrails for any AI agents (or LLMs) assisting with the development of the **Agentic ODI** project. Please adhere to these guidelines to maintain consistency and align with the project's vision.
4: 
5: > **Source of Truth for ODI Methodology**: `knowledge/Strategyn_what_is_Outcome_Driven_Innovation.pdf` by Anthony W. Ulwick (Strategyn). All ODI concepts in this project are grounded in that document. When in doubt, refer agents back to its definitions.
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## 🎯 ODI Methodology Guardrails
10: 
11: This section defines how agents MUST understand and apply Outcome-Driven Innovation within this project. These are not implementation guidelines — they are domain constraints that ensure the system reflects the ODI methodology correctly.
12: 
13: ### What is Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI)?
14: 
15: ODI is a strategy and innovation process rooted in the **Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD)** theory. Its core premise is: **people buy products and services to get a "job" done**. A "job" is the functional process a person is trying to execute — it remains stable over time, while products and technologies are point-in-time solutions that eventually become obsolete.
16: 
17: ODI achieves an **86% innovation success rate** by replacing guesswork with a rigorous, data-driven framework grounded in measurable customer needs.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ### Stage 1: Define the Market and the Job-to-be-Done
22: 
23: - A **market** is defined as: **a group of people + the functional job they are trying to get done** (e.g., "parents trying to pass on life lessons to children").
24: - A **Job-to-be-Done** is the core functional unit of analysis. It is NOT a product, solution, or feature — it is a stable human goal.
25: - **Agent rule**: Before anything else, the agent MUST help the user define the Job-to-be-Done. If no Job exists, use `add_job` to capture it. If one exists already, use `get_jobs()` to check first.
26: - ❌ **Never skip this stage**. No outcomes, steps, or scoring can be meaningful without a well-defined Job.
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ### Stage 2: Uncover Desired Outcomes
31: 
32: - **Desired outcomes** are the metrics customers use to measure success when getting a job done. They are the "needs" in ODI.
33: - Qualitative interviews typically uncover **50–150 desired outcome statements**.
34: - **Correct outcome statement format** (must be enforced when capturing user input):
35: 
36:   > `[Direction] + [Unit of Measure] + [Object of Control] + [Contextual Clarifier]`
37: 
38:   - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the time it takes to determine if the corn seeds are germinating."*
39:   - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the likelihood of damaging the surface when cutting."*
40:   - ❌ **Bad**: *"Make it faster"* — too vague, no direction, no measurable unit.
41:   - ❌ **Bad**: *"I want a notification"* — this is a solution/feature, not an outcome.
42: 
43: - **Agent rule**: Guide the user to express outcomes using this exact format. Reject or reframe vague statements before calling `add_outcome`. Always capture `importance` and `satisfaction` scores (1–10 scale) to enable opportunity scoring.
44: 
45: ---
46: 
47: ### Stage 3: Inventory the Job (Universal Job Map)
48: 
49: - All functional jobs decompose into **8 universal process steps** (the Universal Job Map):
50:   1. **Define** — Plan what needs to be done; select goals or resources
51:   2. **Locate** — Gather the inputs, information, or resources needed
52:   3. **Prepare** — Set up and organize everything required
53:   4. **Confirm** — Validate readiness; decide whether to proceed
54:   5. **Execute** — Perform the core task
55:   6. **Monitor** — Verify and track performance while executing
56:   7. **Modify** — Adjust or update based on feedback
57:   8. **Conclude** — Store, finish, or dispose of outputs
58: 
59: - **Agent rule**: When a user is decomposing a job into steps, reference these 8 universal stages as a guide. Steps captured via `add_step` should map to or be inspired by these universal phases. Use `get_job_map` to visualize the ordered structure.
60: - ❌ **Do not build the Job Map before capturing outcome statements** — outcomes define *what success looks like*; the job map defines *where in the process* that success matters.
61: 
62: ---
63: 
64: ### Stage 4: Discover Where the Market is Underserved (Opportunity Scoring)
65: 
66: - Each desired outcome is rated by customers on two dimensions:
67:   - **Importance** (1–10): How important is this outcome to the customer?
68:   - **Satisfaction** (1–10): How satisfied are customers with current solutions?
69: 
70: - **Opportunity Algorithm** (must be implemented correctly):
71: 
72:   ```
73:   Opportunity Score = Importance + Max(Importance - Satisfaction, 0)
74:   ```
75: 
76: - **Interpretation**:
77:   - **Score > 10**: Underserved need — significant innovation opportunity.
78:   - **Score 10**: Appropriately served — maintain, don't over-invest.
79:   - **Score < 10**: Overserved — potential for disruption via lower-cost alternatives.
80: 
81: - **Agent rule**: Always compute and surface the opportunity score when both `importance` and `satisfaction` are provided. Highlight outcomes scoring **> 10** as the highest priority innovation targets. Use `get_outcomes(job_id)` to review the full opportunity landscape.
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ### Stage 5: Outcome-Based Market Segmentation
86: 
87: - ODI does **not** use demographic segmentation (age, gender, region). Instead it segments the market by **which outcomes are underserved** for each group.
88: - Segments can be:
89:   - **Underserved** — high opportunity scores, want more from existing products
90:   - **Overserved** — over-investing in outcomes that aren't critical; target for disruption
91:   - **Appropriately served** — satisfied; maintain current value
92: 
93: - **Agent rule**: When the user has collected outcomes with scores, help them identify outcome clusters that represent distinct market segments. This drives targeted innovation strategy.
94: 
95: ---
96: 
97: ### Stage 6: Formulate an Innovation Strategy
98: 
99: Based on the opportunity analysis, there are three strategic paths:
100: 
101: | Strategy | When to use |
102: |---|---|
103: | **Differentiated** | Improve existing products to address high-opportunity underserved outcomes |
104: | **Disruptive** | Create low-cost solutions for overserved segments that don't need all existing features |
105: | **New-Market** | Design products for a new job that is entirely unaddressed |
106: 
107: - **Agent rule**: When the opportunity landscape is clear (outcomes scored, segments identified), guide the user to select a strategy path and align their innovation roadmap accordingly.
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: ### ⚠️ ODI Behavioral Guardrails for the Agent
112: 
113: These are absolute constraints the agent must respect:
114: 
115: | DO | DON'T |
116: |---|---|
117: | Always start by defining or confirming the Job-to-be-Done | Jump to solutions, features, or product ideas before the job is defined |
118: | Guide outcome statements with the correct format | Accept vague or solution-framed statements as valid outcomes |
119: | Compute opportunity scores when importance + satisfaction are available | Skip scoring or calculate it incorrectly |
120: | Reference the Universal Job Map when decomposing jobs | Invent arbitrary step structures disconnected from the 8 universal stages |
121: | Use outcome-based logic to identify market segments | Use demographics or assumptions to segment the market |
122: | Treat outcomes as stable, measurable success metrics | Confuse outcomes with features, preferences, or solutions |
123: | Call `get_odi_framework_guidelines` when stage guidance is needed | Guess at which stage comes next |
124: 
125: ---
126: 
127: ## 🛠 Technology Stack & Tools
128: - **Language**: Python 3.10+
129: - **MCP Framework**: `fastmcp` (Server and Client)
130: - **ASGI Server**: `uvicorn`
131: - **HTTP Client**: `httpx`
132: - **UI / Chat Client**: `streamlit`
133: - **LLM Client**: `openai` (OpenAI-compatible, used with Ollama locally)
134: - **Concurrency**: `asyncio`
135: - **Data Modeling / Validation**: `pydantic`
136: 
137: ---
138: 
139: ## 📄 README Maintenance Guardrail
140: 
141: `README.md` is the **primary human-facing entry point** for this project: a short,
142: high-level front door aimed at both users and developers. Detailed material lives
143: in `docs/` and is linked from the README. The agent MUST keep both current at all
144: times.
145: 
146: ### When to update
147: 
148: Update the relevant file whenever any of the following change:
149: 
150: | Change type | Where to update |
151: |---|---|
152: | New or removed Python file / package | `README.md` **Code Overview** |
153: | New dependency added (`pip install ...`) | `README.md` **Quick Start → Prerequisites** |
154: | New way to run the project | `README.md` **Quick Start** and `docs/living-studio.md` |
155: | New MCP tool or capability | `README.md` **Code Overview** / relevant doc |
156: | New CLI command or flag | `docs/cli.md` |
157: | New connector kind | `docs/connectors.md` |
158: | New workflow or agent instruction | `docs/living-studio.md` |
159: | Deployment URL or cloud setup changes | `docs/deployment.md` |
160: | Roadmap item completed or added | `docs/roadmap.md` |
161: | Test layout or coverage changes | `docs/development.md` |
162: 
163: ### Rules
164: 
165: - ✅ **Update docs in the same task** as the change that triggered it — never defer to a follow-up.
166: - ✅ **Keep README short**: it stays a high-level orientation page. Push detail into `docs/` and link to it rather than growing the README.
167: - ✅ **Keep the Quick Start accurate**: always reflect `python -m client.run` as the recommended launch command.
168: - ✅ **Keep Prerequisites up to date**: add any new `pip install` dependency immediately.
169: - ✅ **Mark Roadmap items `[x]` when completed** — do not leave stale unchecked items.
170: - ❌ **Never leave the README or `docs/` in a stale state** where documented commands or files no longer match the codebase.
171: 
172: ---
173: 
174: ## 🚧 Core Development Guardrails
175: 
176: ### 1. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Implementation
177: - **Library Choice**: ALWAYS use [`fastmcp`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) for building the MCP architecture. Avoid using the lower-level Anthropic `mcp` SDK directly unless there is a hyper-specific edge case that `fastmcp` does not support.
178: - **Transport Protocol**: The project is currently prototyping with **HTTP transport** (not stdio). 
179:   - The server should be initialized using `mcp.run(transport="http", ...)`.
180:   - The client must connect to the HTTP endpoint (e.g., `http://localhost:8000/mcp`).
181: - **Tool Creation**: 
182:   - Register tools on the server using the `@mcp.tool` decorator.
183:   - **CRITICAL**: Provide comprehensive docstrings and strict Python type hints for every tool parameter. Explain exactly what the tool does and what data it expects, as this metadata is fed directly to the LLM for tool discovery.
184:   - **Capability Synchronization**: Whenever you add, modify, or remove an MCP tool in `mcp_server/src/mcp_server/mcp_server.py`, you **MUST** simultaneously update the `get_capabilities` tool's human-readable return string to ensure the capability set exactly matches the code.
185: 
186: ### 2. Async / Client Practices
187: - Use `asyncio` for client execution and IO-bound tool operations.
188: - Always use the `fastmcp.Client` securely within an asynchronous context manager (`async with client:`) to ensure connections are efficiently managed and closed.
189: 
190: ### 3. Data Schema & Persistence (ODI Domain)
191: - Define all Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) entities (e.g., *Jobs*, *Steps*, *Desired Outcomes*, *Opportunity Scores*) using `pydantic` models.
192: - When expanding the server to accept complex payloads or to query data, utilize these Pydantic models for built-in type validation and schema enforcement before the server processes the request.
193: 
194: ### 4. General Philosophy
195: - **Separation of Concerns**: Isolate the ODI data logic/retrieval from the MCP server tooling logic.
196: - **Agentic Purpose**: Remember that the tools being built are meant to be consumed by autonomous agents. Design tool interfaces that are intuitive for an LLM to call and interpret.
197: - **External connectors**: Integrations live in the `connectors/` workspace package. New kinds implement `connectors.protocol.Connector` and register via `register_kind`. Do not write ingested records into `jobs_db` / outcomes unless a later mapping task says so.
198: - **MCP client vs ODI server**: The ODI FastMCP **server** exposes product tools. The MCP **client connector** uses `fastmcp.Client` over HTTP to ingest data from *external* MCP servers. Prefer in-memory `Client(server)` tests for that connector, same as server tests.
199: 
200: ### 5. Testing Strategy (FastMCP)
201: - **First-Class Documentation**: Treat tests as living documentation that demonstrate how features work while protecting against regressions.
202: - **Speed & Isolation**: Tests must be fast (< 1s) and self-contained. Use `@pytest.mark.integration` or `@pytest.mark.client_process` for slower, integration, or resource-dependent tests.
203: - **Structure**: This repo is a uv workspace. Mirror each project's code structure in its own `tests/` directory (e.g., `mcp_server/src/mcp_server/mcp_server.py` -> `mcp_server/tests/test_server_tools.py`, `connectors/src/connectors/mcp/connector.py` -> `connectors/tests/test_mcp_connector.py`).
204: - **Atomic Tests**: Each test must verify exactly one specific behavior with clear intent in test names and assertions. Avoid multi-behavior tests.
205: - **In-Memory Testing (Preferred)**: Favor testing functionality deterministically by passing the `FastMCP` server directly into the `Client(server)` instance. This runs in-memory without network overhead for deterministic and lightning-fast execution.
206: - **Transport Testing (When Needed)**: For HTTP/SSE network transport tests, prefer the isolated in-process `fastmcp.utilities.tests.run_server_async(server)` context manager over subprocess testing (which uses `run_server_in_process` and is slower to debug).
207: - **Data Assertions**: Utilize `inline-snapshot` (`snapshot()`) for assessing complex data structures like tool API JSON schemas or expected responses.

1: # Running The Living Studio
2: 
3: **The Living Studio** is the conversational GUI for Outcome-Driven Innovation:
4: an interactive Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map, WYSIWYG Impact
5: Simulation, and Causal Lineage inspection, paired with an autonomous agent
6: connected to the MCP server.
7: 
8: The Studio runs three ways. All of them serve the same SPA, which talks only to
9: the sidecar on `http://127.0.0.1:8100` — the SPA never contacts MCP or the LLM
10: directly.
11: 
12: ## Architecture
13: 
14: ```text
15: ┌────────────────────────────┐  /api (JSON)  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
16: │  Living Studio SPA         │ ────────────▶ │  local_server (sidecar)       │
17: │  React + TS + Vite         │  /api/chat    │  FastAPI on 127.0.0.1:8100    │
18: │  (browser or Tauri webview)│ ◀──────────── │  - config / health / canvas   │
19: └────────────────────────────┘  SSE stream   │  - steps / outcomes (via MCP) │
20:                                              │  - /api/chat (LLM tool-loop)  │
21:                                              └───────────────┬───────────────┘
22:                                                              │ MCP (HTTP)
23:                                                              ▼
24:                                              ┌───────────────────────────────┐
25:                                              │  mcp_server  :8000/mcp        │
26:                                              └───────────────────────────────┘
27:                                                              ▲
28:                                                              │ OpenAI-compatible
29:                                              ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
30:                                              │  Your local LLM backend       │
31:                                              └───────────────────────────────┘
32: ```
33: 
34: ## 1. Web — production build (recommended for a quick look)
35: 
36: ```bash
37: npm --prefix studio run build   # build the SPA into studio/dist
38: python -m client.run            # starts MCP :8000 + sidecar :8100
39: ```
40: 
41: | Service | URL |
42: |---|---|
43: | MCP Server | http://localhost:8000/mcp |
44: | Living Studio | http://127.0.0.1:8100 |
45: 
46: `python -m client.run` starts both processes concurrently; press **Ctrl+C** to
47: stop both.
48: 
49: ## 2. Web — dev with hot reload
50: 
51: Vite proxies `/api` to the sidecar:
52: 
53: ```bash
54: npm --prefix studio run dev:full   # MCP + sidecar + Vite together
55: # open http://localhost:5173
56: ```
57: 
58: ## 3. Desktop — Tauri 2
59: 
60: The app spawns the MCP server and sidecar itself:
61: 
62: ```bash
63: npm --prefix studio run tauri dev     # dev window
64: npm --prefix studio run tauri build   # bundles: .deb / .AppImage (Linux), .app / .dmg (macOS), .msi / .exe (Windows)
65: ```
66: 
67: > [!NOTE]
68: > **Tauri prerequisites.** The desktop build needs the WebKitGTK toolchain and
69: > Rust 1.90+. On Debian/Ubuntu:
70: >
71: > ```bash
72: > sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev build-essential pkg-config curl wget file \
73: >   libxdo-dev libssl-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf xdg-utils libfuse2t64
74: > ```
75: >
76: > The Tauri CLI ships as the `@tauri-apps/cli` npm dev dependency
77: > (`npm --prefix studio run tauri`). The sidecar is launched with
78: > `uv run python -m …` from the repository root; if the app cannot locate the
79: > repo root, set `AGENTIC_ODI_REPO_ROOT`.
80: 
81: ## Desktop signing & updater secrets
82: 
83: Self-updating and code signing are **env-driven**: if a secret is absent, an
84: unsigned artifact is produced instead of failing. CI reads these from GitHub
85: Actions secrets.
86: 
87: | Secret | Purpose |
88: |---|---|
89: | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` | Signs updater artifacts (`.sig`) and the `latest.json` manifest. A tagged release fails loudly without it. Generate with `npm --prefix studio run tauri signer generate`. |
90: | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD` | Password for the private key (optional when the key has none). |
91: | `APPLE_CERTIFICATE` / `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | macOS Developer ID certificate (base64 `.p12`) and its password. |
92: | `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` | macOS signing identity. |
93: | `APPLE_ID` / `APPLE_PASSWORD` / `APPLE_TEAM_ID` | macOS notarization credentials. |
94: | `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE` / `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | Windows Authenticode PFX (base64) and its password; imported by CI and injected into the bundle config. |
95: 
96: Releases are published by `.github/workflows/tauri-release.yml` when a `v*` tag
97: is pushed. The desktop app checks for updates on startup and via
98: **Settings → Check for updates**.
99: 
100: ### Managing the updater signing key
101: 
102: The updater key pair authenticates release artifacts so an installed app can
103: verify that an auto-update genuinely came from you. The **public** key is
104: embedded in `studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` (`plugins.updater.pubkey`) and is
105: safe to commit. The **private** key must never be committed, logged, printed in
106: CI, or attached to a build artifact.
107: 
108: 1. **Generate a key pair** (only if you need a new one). Leave `-p ""` for a
109:    passwordless key, or pass a password and remember it:
110: 
111:    ```bash
112:    npm --prefix studio run tauri signer generate -- -w ./living-studio.key -p "" -f
113:    ```
114: 
115:    This writes `living-studio.key` (private, `0600`) and `living-studio.key.pub`
116:    (public).
117: 
118: 2. **Paste the public key** into `studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`:
119: 
120:    ```jsonc
121:    {
122:      "plugins": {
123:        "updater": {
124:          "endpoints": ["https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/latest.json"],
125:          "pubkey": "<contents of living-studio.key.pub>"
126:        }
127:      }
128:    }
129:    ```
130: 
131: 3. **Store the private key outside the repository** (the repo root is
132:    git-tracked; a sibling directory is not), with restricted permissions:
133: 
134:    ```bash
135:    mkdir -p ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys && chmod 700 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys
136:    mv living-studio.key ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/
137:    chmod 600 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key
138:    ```
139: 
140:    Move it to a long-term secret store (password manager, 1Password/Bitwarden/
141:    Vault, or a private encrypted backup) when you decide where that lives.
142:    Losing it means future releases can no longer be signed for existing
143:    installs.
144: 
145: 4. **Add the private key as a GitHub Actions secret** (Settings → Secrets and
146:    variables → Actions → New repository secret), or via the CLI:
147: 
148:    ```bash
149:    gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY < ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key
150:    gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD --body ""   # only if you set a password
151:    ```
152: 
153: 5. **Verify** the secrets exist (values are never displayed):
154: 
155:    ```bash
156:    gh secret list
157:    ```
158: 
159: 6. **Rotate** by repeating steps 1–4, then publishing a release signed with the
160:    new key. Existing installs still verify against the public key compiled into
161:    their binary, so keep the old private key usable and publish the new public
162:    key ahead of the cut-over.
163: 
164: > [!CAUTION]
165: > If the private key leaks, treat auto-updates as compromised: generate a new
166: > pair, rotate the Actions secret, and publish a freshly signed release.
167: 
168: > [!IMPORTANT]
169: > **Migration note.** The Streamlit UI (`client/src/client/app.py`) has been
170: > removed. The Living Studio now lives in `studio/` (browser SPA + Tauri desktop
171: > app) and is served by the `local_server` sidecar on port **8100** (previously
172: > Streamlit's `8501`). Start everything with `python -m client.run`. All
173: > `AGENTIC_ODI_*` environment variable names, the demo dataset, and the ODI
174: > formulas are unchanged.
175: 
176: ## Rich responses
177: 
178: The copilot does not only talk. When a surface carries the evidence better than a
179: paragraph, the agent renders one **inline in the conversation**: a scored
180: outcome, a ranked opportunity board, a before/after simulation of a bet, a
181: customer quote with its lineage, the eight-stage job map, or a decision record.
182: Three properties keep this safe and cheap to extend:
183: 
184: - **The catalog is closed and owned by the SPA.**
185:   `apps/studio/src/ui/catalog.ts` declares nine primitives and six cards, their
186:   JSON Schema props, and the description the model reads. There is no HTML, no
187:   eval, and no third-party component in the path.
188: - **The sidecar is catalog-agnostic.** The SPA sends the catalog with each turn;
189:   the sidecar derives the `render_ui` tool schema from it, validates what comes
190:   back, and streams a `ui` SSE event. Invalid props return to the model as a tool
191:   result naming the exact violation, so a fumbled prop is corrected in the same
192:   reply. A client that sends no catalog never sees the tool.
193: - **Cards are views, never actors.** Every button is an `intent` string that the
194:   agent receives as the user's next message — one authority, one audit trail.
195: 
196: A surface is one node tree, streamed as one event:
197: 
198: ```json
199: {
200:   "type": "outcome-card",
201:   "props": {
202:     "id": "O-1",
203:     "statement": "Minimize the time it takes to propagate secrets across environments",
204:     "importance": 9,
205:     "satisfaction": 3
206:   }
207: }
208: ```
209: 
210: The opportunity score is computed from importance and satisfaction when the
211: agent omits it, so the ODI formula has exactly one home (`src/lib/odi.ts`).
212: Unknown component types degrade to a quiet fallback; a tree that fails
213: validation is dropped whole, and the surrounding prose still reads.
214: 
215: Run the sidecar without a model and the demo still renders real cards — that
216: path is what a first-run user reaches after the tour, and it exercises every
217: card type in CI.
218: 
219: ### Adding a surface
220: 
221: 1. Add an entry to `CATALOG` in `apps/studio/src/ui/catalog.ts` — props as a
222:    JSON Schema subset, plus the description the model will read.
223: 2. Register the component in `apps/studio/src/ui/registry.ts`.
224: 3. Implement it in `apps/studio/src/ui/cards.tsx` (domain shape) or
225:    `apps/studio/src/ui/primitives.tsx` (composition).
226: 4. Run `npm --prefix apps/studio test`. The `registry parity` test fails if the
227:    catalog and the registry drift apart.
228: 
229: No server change is needed, and no new dependency.
230: 
231: ## First-run wizard
232: 
233: A new user is greeted by a four-step tour before the canvas: what the studio is,
234: which of the four starting points they want, the live state of their sidecar /
235: MCP server / model (with inline repair when the model is down), and the exact
236: first prompt the copilot will receive. The last step sends that prompt and
237: reveals the canvas at the matching tab, so the tour ends in real work.
238: 
239: The tour is skippable (footer action or `Escape`) and resumable: progress is
240: stored after every step in `localStorage["studio.onboarding"]`. Replay it any
241: time from **Settings → Replay the welcome tour** — the header's settings control
242: makes that reachable from the first-run shell.
243: 
244: Everything lives in `apps/studio/src/onboarding/`:
245: 
246: | File | Role |
247: |---|---|
248: | `content.ts` | Steps and goal copy as typed data — the only place the words live |
249: | `machine.ts` | Pure state transitions, no React or storage |
250: | `storage.ts` | Versioned, defensive `localStorage` persistence |
251: | `OnboardingProvider.tsx` | Auto-open, persistence, replay |
252: | `FirstRunWizard.tsx`, `steps.tsx`, `onboarding.css` | The dialog |
253: | `../features/flags.ts` | The `firstRunWizard` toggle |
254: 
255: The app only wires the provider and the wizard into `App.tsx`; the canvas, chat,
256: and API code are untouched.
257: 
258: ### Toggling the wizard
259: 
260: `firstRunWizard` defaults to on. Resolution order, highest first:
261: 
262: | Source | Example | Use |
263: |---|---|---|
264: | Query parameter | `?flags=firstRunWizard:off` | QA a build without rebuilding |
265: | Local override | `localStorage["studio.flags.firstRunWizard"] = "off"` | Per-browser opt-out |
266: | Build environment | `VITE_STUDIO_FIRST_RUN_WIZARD=off npm --prefix apps/studio run build` | Ship it dark |
267: | Default | on | |
268: 
269: Accepted values are `1`/`0`, `true`/`false`, `on`/`off`, `yes`/`no`, and
270: `enabled`/`disabled`. With the flag off, no dialog renders, no onboarding state
271: is written, and Settings hides the replay action.
272: 
273: ## Connecting an LLM
274: 
275: The Studio needs an OpenAI-compatible LLM backend with tool-calling support to
276: drive the agent. For a fully local setup, see
277: [Local LLM Backend](local-llm.md).
278: 
279: ## Agent-Driven Testing
280: 
281: Type `/dev` in the AI assistant to trigger the full automated workflow: it starts
282: both processes, opens the browser, sends a test message, and reports the results.
283: 
284: Type `/test` to have the agent run all tests and report the results
285: automatically.

(End of file - total 285 lines)
</content>

I've now reviewed the full client studio surface end-to-end. Here's my review, a Steve Jobs filter pass, and a concrete improvement plan.

## Findings — mapped to the code

| Your point | Where it lives | What's happening |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Landing text hard to read / no focus** | `StudioHeader.tsx:10-15`, `ChatCopilot.tsx:136-141`, `StudioContext.tsx:40-43` | Post-wizard shell (engagement 0) shows header title **"The Living Studio \| Outcome-Driven Innovation"** + subtitle *"A Canvas of Human Intent. Zero file trees. Real-time causality."* + 3 pills, then chat head *"Copilot"* + caption *"Speak your intent…"*, then welcome **"Welcome to The Living Studio…"** — three naming blocks competing for attention; no visual stage. |
| **2. "Living Studio" twice** | `StudioHeader.tsx:11`, `StudioContext.tsx:41`, `CanvasTabs.tsx:47-51`, `SettingsPanel.tsx:22,119` | "The Living Studio" appears in the header title **and** the welcome message simultaneously; plus the sync bar says *"Living Studio Canvas ready"* and settings says *"Living Studio Controls"* when they open. |
| **3. Too many items initially** | `ChatCopilot.tsx:9-19`, `StudioContext.tsx:45-62`, `SettingsPanel.tsx:11` | 5 action buttons at once (2 welcome-card actions + 3 quick pills) — with **"Define a job" and "ODI guidelines" each duplicated**. Settings drawer defaults open (`useState(true)`) exposing 4 inputs + a full About section. |
| **4. Circulating text too verbose** | `CanvasTabs.tsx:45-58` | Status cycles *"⚡ Syncing with Living Studio Canvas \& FastMCP…"* → *"🟢 Local Studio Prototype Loaded"* → *"✨ Living Studio Canvas ready"*, plus a `source: <badge> · cached · updating…` line — 8+ words of decorative churn above the canvas. |
| **5. Changes too often** | `ChatCopilot.tsx:21-25`, `CanvasTabs.tsx:45-58` | The thinking label rotates *"Reaching the model" → "Loading your tools" → "Thinking"* on every SSE status event; the sync bar flutters on every canvas refresh. Neither carries signal — it's noise. |
| **6. No focus frame on the conversation** | `theme.css:140` (`studio-layout`) | A bare 2-col grid; the chat has no container border, so the conversation competes visually with the canvas, header, and settings instead of taking the stage. |

## The Steve Jobs filter

I ran every element through: *is it essential? does it defer to content? could it be simpler?*

| Element | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Header subtitle *"A Canvas of Human Intent…"* | **Cut** | Decorative; the caption + welcome carry purpose. |
| "ODI Framework v1.0" pill | **Cut** | Version noise, not a user concern. |
| Three status pills | **Fold to one** | LLM+MCP state is one question: live or demo. |
| "Living Studio" in welcome message | **Cut** | Name belongs in the header, once. |
| "Living Studio" in settings/about/sync bar | **Cut** | Header already establishes identity. |
| Welcome-card action buttons | **Cut** | Redundant with the pills below. |
| "ODI guidelines" quick pill | **Cut** | Reference material, not a first move. |
| "Simulate a bet" quick pill | **Cut** (deferred) | Needs an outcome first — not an initial move. |
| "Define a job" quick pill | **Keep** (single source of truth) | The clearest first move. |
| "Score the outcomes" quick pill | **Keep** | The other natural entry point. |
| Settings drawer open-by-default | **Close by default** | Complexity hidden until summoned. |
| Sync-bar emoji cycling + source badge | **Replace** with one stable line. |
| Thinking-phase rotation | **Replace** with "Working…" + the dot pulse. |

## Concrete recommendations (file:line → change)

**A. One clear identity — header** (`StudioHeader.tsx:10-15`)
- Title → `"The Living Studio"` only. Drop the `| Outcome-Driven Innovation` suffix and drop the subtitle line.
- `StudioHeader.tsx:17-28` — replace the 3 pills with **one** consolidated status pill: `"🟢 Live"` / `"🟡 Demo mode"`. Drop the "ODI Framework v1.0" pill.

**B. Drop the duplicate name — welcome message** (`StudioContext.tsx:40-43`)
- New: `"A living map of human progress. Tell me what your customers struggle with and I'll answer with evidence."` — no "Welcome to The Living Studio."

**C. Stage the conversation with a border** (`theme.css`)
- Add a `.chat-frame` bordered container around `.chat-copilot` (1px `var(--studio-border)`, radius `--studio-radius`, subtle shadow) so the conversation is the clear stage. Keep the canvas in a lighter frame. Update `studio-layout` so the chat column carries the prominent frame.

**D. One path forward — first impression** (`ChatCopilot.tsx:9-19`, `StudioContext.tsx:45-62`)
- Reduce quick pills 3→2: **Define a job**, **Score the outcomes**. Drop "Simulate a bet" and "ODI guidelines".
- Make the welcome card **text-only** — drop its two `actions` buttons (`StudioContext.tsx:49-60`), keeping just the prose. The 2 pills + input are the path; no duplicated button.

**E. Defer complexity — settings** (`SettingsPanel.tsx:11,19,22,119`)
- `useState(true)` → `useState(false)`.
- `"🎛️ Living Studio Controls"` → `"⚙️ Controls"`.
- `"About the Living Studio"` → `"About this canvas"`; `aria-label` `"Living Studio controls"` → `"Studio controls"`.

**F. Stable, quiet status — circulating text** (`CanvasTabs.tsx:45-58`, `ChatCopilot.tsx:21-25`)
- Sync bar → a single line: *"Canvas synced"* at idle, or a tiny spinner + *"Syncing…"* while loading. Remove the emoji cycling, the `source-badge`, and the `cached · updating…` badge.
- Thinking label → single word `"Working…"` (keep the 3-dot pulse as the only motion).

## Jobs pass verdict

The cuts above remove 4 redundant labels, 2 duplicated buttons, 1 decorative subtitle, 1 version pill, and an entire emoji-cycling status system — while preserving every capability. The result: a header that names the product once, a conversation in a clear frame, two honest starting moves, and a quiet sync/thinking state that no longer fights for attention. That's the direction Jobs would sign off on.

**One scope question before I write the design doc:** I'm treating "the landing page" as the main studio shell (post-wizard). Should I also tighten the first-run wizard's copy (e.g. its "The Living Studio" wordmark + the verbose welcome lead), or leave the wizard as the focused place to choose a goal and trim only the main shell? And for the border treatment — do you want the canvas to **dim/fold** when idle (so the chat is unmistakably the stage), or stay present but in a lighter frame?
Tackle the wider scope you suggested
Good — I'll extend the Jobs pass to cover the first-run wizard too, since that's the user's true first impression. Let me verify a couple of wizard details before finalizing the wider plan.

10:  * Versioned, defensive persistence for the tour. A malformed or outdated record

22:   if (typeof window === "undefined") {
23:     return null;
24:   }
25:   try {
26:     return window.localStorage;
27:   } catch {
28:     return null;
29:   }

33:   return typeof value === "string" && GOAL_IDS.has(value);
34: }

37:   let parsed: unknown;
38:   try {
39:     parsed = JSON.parse(raw);
40:   } catch {
41:     return null;
42:   }
43:   if (typeof parsed !== "object" || parsed === null) {
44:     return null;
45:   }
46:

48:   if (candidate.version !== ONBOARDING_VERSION) {
49:     return null;
50:   }
51:   if (!STATUSES.includes(candidate.status as OnboardingStatus)) {
52:     return null;
53:   }
54:   if (
55:     typeof candidate.step !== "number" ||
56:     !Number.isInteger(candidate.step) ||
57:     candidate.step < 0 ||
58:     candidate.step >= STEPS.length
59:   ) {
60:     return null;
61:   }
62:   if (candidate.goal !== null && !isGoalId(candidate.goal)) {
63:     return null;

66:   if (candidate.step > GOAL_STEP_INDEX && !isGoalId(candidate.goal)) {
67:     return null;
68:   }
69: 
70:   return createOnboardingState({
71:     status: candidate.status as OnboardingStatus,
72:     step: candidate.step,
73:     goal: (candidate.goal as GoalId | null) ?? null,
74:   });
75: }

| Element | Jobs verdict | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Header subtitle `StudioHeader.tsx:13-15` | **Cut** | Decorative; caption + welcome carry purpose. |
| "ODI Framework v1.0" pill `StudioHeader.tsx:18` | **Cut** | Version noise. |

Canvas column gets a lighter `.canvas-frame`. The chat becomes the clearly-bounded stage; canvas is the supporting pane.

<skill_content name="writing-plans">
# Skill: writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans

# Living Studio First-Impression & Readability UX Design

**Date:** 2026-10-21
**Status:** Approved for implementation
**Scope:** The Living Studio's header, first impression / first-run shell, conversation framing, status surfaces, and copy.

## Intent & Why

The first moment a user reaches the Studio must point unambiguously at the one
thing that matters: the conversation. Today the opening screen carries the
product name in several places at once, surfaces a verbose status bar that
churns, opens a settings panel full of inputs by default, and offers five
near-duplicate starting buttons. The result is hard to read and unclear to
focus.

This change strips that noise so the eye has exactly one place to land — the
chat — and every label says what it means the first time, once.

**North star:** *Say the name once. Frame the conversation. Give one first move.*

## Goals

- The product name ("The Living Studio") appears exactly once on screen at any
  moment, in the header.
- No decorative subtitle or version pill competes with the header.
- A single consolidated status pill replaces the three current status pills.
- The welcome message does not restate the product name.
- The conversation lives in a clear bordered frame; the canvas is secondary.
- The first impression offers the fewest honest starting moves (two starter
  pills + the input), with no duplicated buttons.
- The settings drawer opens collapsed; its heading drops the redundant name.
- Status text is quiet: a single stable line for canvas sync, and a single
  "Working…" label for the thinking phase (motion stays as the dot pulse only).
- The first-run wizard keeps its four honest goal choices and focus trap, but
  its copy drops the product-name echo and tightens its lead line.

## Non-Goals

- A full visual redesign. Reuse the existing dark design language.
- Changing the ODI domain model, scoring, or MCP tool surface.
- Changing the canvas tab set or the canvas data model.
- Adding new features, surfaces, or capabilities.

## Experience

### The shell, post-wizard (engagement 0 → 1 → 2)

**Before.** Header reads "The Living Studio | Outcome-Driven Innovation"
plus subtitle "A Canvas of Human Intent. Zero file trees. Real-time causality."
plus three pills ("ODI Framework v1.0", LLM state, MCP state). Below it the
chat head reads "Copilot / Speak your intent…", then the welcome message
"Welcome to The Living Studio…". The settings drawer opens by default with
four inputs and an "About the Living Studio" section. The canvas sync bar
cycles emoji-laden text and a "source / cached · updating…" badge.

**After.** Header reads just "The Living Studio" and one status pill
("Live" / "Demo mode"). No subtitle. The chat is wrapped in a bordered
`.chat-frame` so it is the clear stage. The welcome message is a single
concise sentence with no name restatement. Starter pills reduced to
"Define a job" and "Score the outcomes". The welcome card becomes pure
intro text (its two action buttons are removed — they duplicated the pills).
The settings drawer starts collapsed with heading "Controls". The sync bar
is one stable line ("Canvas synced" / "Updating…"). The thinking phase is
one stable label ("Working…") backed by the existing pulse.

### The first-run wizard

**Before.** Step 1 wordmark says "The Living Studio"; the step-1 lead then
says "The Living Studio helps you…" — a name echo. The lead is 24 words.

**After.** Wordmark stays (it is the only name shown during the tour). The
lead drops the name and is tightened to one concise sentence. The four goal
cards and the three-moves list are kept — they are the product's first
decision, not clutter. The wizard's accessibility behavior (focus trap,
Escape to skip, Tab containment) is unchanged.

## Constraints

- Keep all existing vitest tests green. Where copy changes break an assertion,
  update the assertion to the new copy — but never weaken a behavioral test.
- No emojis in product chrome: remove emojis from the status pills, the sync
  bar, and any new status text. (Aligns with the project's existing
  "No emojis in product chrome" convention.)
- Local-first: no new network calls, no new runtime dependencies.
- Update `docs/living-studio.md` in the same task if user-facing copy or
  behavior changes that it describes.

## Acceptance

- Header renders exactly one visible occurrence of "Living Studio".
- Settings drawer starts collapsed.
- Sync bar renders a single line and never shows the cycling emoji text.
- Thinking phase renders a single stable label.
- Quick pills are exactly "Define a job" and "Score the outcomes".
- Welcome card renders no action buttons.
- Wizard step-1 lead does not contain "The Living Studio".
- `npm --prefix apps/studio run typecheck`, `lint`, and `test` all pass.
